claims.text: As-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exhibit copper segregation at their surfaces.
Local surface chemical inhomogeneities primarily govern premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Surface enrichment of copper is the particularly important chemical inhomogeneity governing the particles' thermal response.
Short annealing near 0.9Tm followed by rapid quenching will reduce copper surface segregation.
Annealing for 10–30 seconds near 0.9Tm in an inert atmosphere can homogenize the surface composition while limiting coarsening.
An inert annealing atmosphere prevents oxidation during surface homogenization.
The proposed annealing treatment achieves surface homogenization without causing additional phase transformations.
Rapid quenching freezes in the homogenized chemical state.
Copper has a lower melting point than the other alloy constituents.
Copper enrichment at the nanoparticle surface locally depresses the melting temperature and initiates premelting.
Copper segregation creates a diffusion barrier.
Reducing the diffusion barrier associated with copper segregation shifts premelting onset closer to the intrinsic bulk melting point.
Annealed and quenched nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Annealed and quenched nanoparticles will show less liquid-like surface material before complete melting.
Annealed and quenched nanoparticles will undergo a more spatially uniform and abrupt melting transition.
Copper surface segregation causes earlier and more gradual premelting in the baseline particles.
The proposed mechanism applies mainly to rapidly solidified HEA nanoparticles in which chemical segregation is prominent and at temperatures near but below the bulk melting temperature.
Significant lattice strain or external coatings may supersede copper segregation as the dominant control on melting behavior.

contradictions.description: The conditions field states that annealing achieves homogenization without additional phase transformations, whereas the uncertainty field acknowledges that minor phase transformations may occur during treatment.

The mechanism invokes removal of a copper-created diffusion barrier as part of the reason melting is delayed, but it does not explain why reducing a kinetic barrier to diffusion would suppress rather than facilitate surface disordering or melting.
